The second option is the belief that a rule reasons about people, and it is the source of most disappointed expectations about detection. questions.explanation: A learned baseline is a picture of a world at a particular time, so when the world changes for good the picture is wrong and everything that looks new looks wrong with it. questions.stem: Eradication is complete. Four actions follow before the incident can be closed. Put them in order.

answer.exemplar: Restoring the service settles a question about availability and leaves every other question exactly where it was, and the list of those questions is long enough that treating the outage as the end is how incidents recur quietly for months. The first is whether what caused it is gone, since restoring a system that still has the route in simply makes it available to be used again. The second is whether what the party left behind is gone, and this is a different question from the first, because a foothold can be present on a system that was rebuilt from sound media, in the form of a scheduled task, a second account or a credential that was never changed. The third is whether the party still has access, which is the one most often left open because it feels like a credential problem rather than a recovery problem, and it is not: an unchanged credential is access, and access does not care that the system was restored. The fourth is whether anything else was reached, which is a question about the estate rather than about this host, and it is the one that determines whether the incident was one machine or thirty. So the verification that follows recovery has to be evidence against those four things rather than a check that the service is answering, and it has three properties to be worth anything. It has to look for the specific things that were seen during the incident, since a general health check is satisfied by a system that is compromised in a way the check does not measure. It has to confirm that the route in is shut, which is a different assertion from the one about the foothold and is the one that makes the difference between a system that was cleaned and a weakness that was fixed. And it has to be recorded, because the person who reads this host's record in six months is not going to reconstruct why it was thought to be clean. There is a practical consequence worth stating as well: the confidence to close an incident should come from the verification rather than from the absence of further alerts, since a party who has been removed and a party who has gone quiet produce the same quiet, and the only thing that distinguishes them is a check that was actually run.

answer.exemplar: An acceptance is a transfer, and the reason a transfer works is that somebody is now answerable for the thing and there is a point at which the arrangement is revisited. Those two elements are what separate a decision from a note, and it is worth being precise about how each one fails on its own, because the failures look like tidiness problems and are not. Without a name, the entry records a judgement that nobody owns, which means there is nobody to ask when the circumstances change, and in practice it means the entry is read once during an audit and then never again. An acceptance without a date fails differently and more quietly: it looks like a decision and behaves like a permanent exception, and permanent exceptions are the normal destination of items nobody had the resources to fix, so the register slowly fills with items that are neither being worked nor being decided. Without the evidence behind the judgement, a third problem appears, which is that the entry cannot be revisited even by somebody who wants to, because there is nothing recorded about what was true when the call was made, so six months later the only available reading is that the decision was made about a different situation. There is a fourth element that is often left out and that turns out to matter most in practice, which is the condition that would reverse the acceptance. Something of the form: if this figure moves, or this control is withdrawn, or this assumption stops holding, the acceptance lapses and the item returns. That converts the entry from a statement about the present into a standing instruction, and it is the only part of it that acts without anybody remembering to check. Together the four make an entry that can be handed to a successor, which is the real test of whether a governance artefact works, and the practical test to apply to a register is to pick any entry written two years ago and ask whether a reader could say what would have to be true now for it to still be the right call. If they cannot, the entry recorded a decision that nobody is making any more.

answer.exemplar: The distinguishing property is that in one case something consults the policy at the moment a decision is made, and in the other case nothing does, so the behaviour of the system is the same whether the policy exists or not. That is a testable difference rather than a matter of opinion, and it is worth stating as the test because it disposes of most of the arguments people have about whether a policy is being obeyed. Ask what would change in the running system if the paragraph were deleted, and if the answer is nothing, then compliance depends entirely on every person who ever makes this decision having read it and remembered it, which is a real but much weaker property and one that fails quietly rather than loudly. The evidence that separates the two cases comes in three kinds and they are worth collecting deliberately. The first is a decision record: an audit of what was actually granted, against what the policy would have permitted, which turns a claim into a measurement and which is also the only evidence that would ever reveal a policy that is followed by some people and not others. The second is a negative result, which is stronger than a positive one and is usually available: a request that the policy forbids and the system refused, because a control that has never refused anything has not been shown to work. The third is a discrepancy, and the most useful single artefact a team can produce is the list of grants that would not have been permitted, since that list is simultaneously the evidence that the policy is not enforced and the specification of what to fix. There is a fourth consideration that is about design rather than evidence, and it is why the grant service in the example above is the real finding: a policy enforced by a human being is a policy whose strength is the strength of the newest member of the team, whereas a policy enforced by the system that makes the decision is a property of the system and survives turnover, absence and pressure. So the practical work is not persuading people to follow the policy but moving the decision into a place that consults it, and the practical test is whether a person who has never heard of the policy would still be stopped by it, which is the same question asked of every control in this subject.

questions.explanation: A classification made under time pressure will vary with the person making it unless the level is a function of stated facts, and the test for a well-built scale is that two teams looking at the same facts would write the same level down. That is a design constraint rather than an aspiration, and it rules out the most common way these scales go wrong, which is to write them in terms of adjectives describing seriousness rather than in terms of what is observably true. The second option removes an ambiguity people actually have, which is who decides, and it leaves the larger one untouched, since two people consulting under pressure will still choose differently. The third is a reasonable instinct and it has the ordering wrong: a response time belongs to a level as a consequence of it, and writing it into the label makes the scale harder to apply because responders have to judge the consequence before they know the facts. The fourth is about recognition rather than consistency, and being fast at applying a scale is not the same as applying it the same way twice.

questions.explanation: The internal audiences are easy to reach because they are in the building, on a rota and reachable by a chat message, so they get told by accident. The external audiences are the ones with obligations attached that start running on facts rather than on decisions, which means the clock is already going while the team is still working out what happened, and the audiences that get missed are the ones nobody inside the organisation has a relationship with: the regulator, the insurer, the police, and the people whose data was involved. The cost is not embarrassment, it is a missed deadline that cannot be recovered afterwards, since the obligation runs from a moment the team did not choose and did not notice. The second option identifies the audience most likely to be over-communicated rather than forgotten, which is its own problem and the opposite one. The third and fourth are real operational concerns and both are cheap to solve internally; the fourth in particular is a genuine gap, since the people taking the calls are the ones who know what the customers are actually asking, and it belongs in the plan for that reason rather than because of a legal clock.

questions.explanation: The awkward property of these duties is that they are triggered by the state of the world rather than by anything the organisation decides, so the organisation does not get to choose its start time and a delay that feels generous while the facts are being established has already been running. That makes preparation into a monitoring problem: write down which facts start each clock, make sure something in the estate would notice when one of them becomes true, and be able to show when it did. The second option is the belief that makes this feel like a decision rather than a fact, and it is the source of most of the missed deadlines, because a team that thinks it controls the start will plan from the point of deciding rather than from the point of knowing. The third confuses the length of the delay with the uncertainty of the trigger, and those are independent: a short delay from a clear trigger is the case to worry about. questions.explanation: A list of names is a lookup table and a set of starting facts is a detector, and the difference matters because of what each one can do on its own. The detector can notice that something has become true, and everything else then follows: the team knows it has an obligation, knows which one, and can begin. The list cannot do that, because it is consulted after somebody has already decided there is something to say, and the person deciding is the person the facts were supposed to inform. In practice this is the difference between a duty that is met and a duty that is met when somebody remembers, and it is why the first style is the one that scales to several jurisdictions, since each jurisdiction's facts can be detected by the same monitoring and each one's list read afterwards. The second option identifies a real piece of work and misplaces its difficulty in time, since the names are knowable now and the facts are knowable only then. The fourth overstates the position: the external bodies set the deadlines, which is exactly why knowing the triggering facts in advance is the part worth preparing.

answer.exemplar: The chain is a commitment, made at one moment, to two things: what each item contained, and the order the items were taken in. The first part is a digest per item, and it answers the question a later reader actually has, which is whether the copy in front of them is the copy that was taken, and it does so without storing the content anywhere else. The second part is what makes the chain a chain rather than a list, because each link is the digest of the previous link together with the next item, so the list cannot be reordered, dropped from the middle, or extended at either end without the change showing up. Verified on a throwaway tree, and the results are worth stating because they are the argument: appending a byte to one file was caught and located at that file, deleting a file was caught at that file, and swapping two files that were both present was caught at the second of the two. Notice what those three have in common, which is that the list stayed the same and the files did not, and notice also what none of them establishes, which is that the list is the right list. Trimming entries off the end of the manifest verified without complaint, because a chain proves the sequence it describes and has nothing to say about whether the description is complete. That is not a defect of the mechanism, it is a boundary of it, and it is why the interesting question about a capture is usually not whether the files are intact but whether the set of files is what somebody would have collected. The same boundary reappears at the other end of the process. These digests can say that the content has not changed and they cannot say who held it, where it was, or what was done to it, because none of that is in the bytes. That is the job of the custody record, and the two together are what make an item usable: the chain answers whether it is the same item, the custody record answers how it got here, and an item with a perfect chain and a gap in its custody has told you it is unaltered and nothing about who has had it. It is worth being clear about the asymmetry that creates, because it is what makes the record worth keeping even when everyone involved is trustworthy: the chain is something a machine can check, the custody record is something only people can attest to, and the weakness of the whole arrangement sits in the part that cannot be verified.

questions.explanation: A per-item digest establishes that the content has not changed and a link over the previous digest establishes the order, so editing, deletion and reordering are all caught and located, as confirmed on a throwaway tree. What it cannot see is an item left off the list, since a chain proves the sequence it describes and not that the description is complete, and it says nothing about custody, which is a separate human record.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two things the chain commits to is checked, and what the chain is not told about.

questions.explanation: The purpose of the record is to make a gap visible. A single handover from a trained examiner to an evidence store is unremarkable, and the value of writing it down is not that this handover is in doubt but that every subsequent handover is on the same footing, so when something is later questioned the record can be read to find the point at which nobody can say. That is the whole design: the record is not there to prove that nothing happened, since a record cannot do that, it is there to localise the part of the history that cannot be accounted for. The second option is a genuine concern and it belongs in the handling instructions rather than in the custody record, which is about the item's journey and not its environment. The third is about the scene rather than the item, and the two diverge as soon as an item is copied, since a copy inherits the chain and the scene does not. The fourth is a real property to record and it is a different record again, and a useful one, but knowing the format was sound says nothing about who has held the item since.
questions.hint: Ask what the record is for when something is later questioned.

questions.explanation: The reason the record is kept is that a reader who cannot account for a stretch of time has no way to tell an innocent explanation from a guilty one, and honesty is not something that can be established from the outside; it can only be recorded in advance by people who had no reason to think it would matter. That is an uncomfortable property of the arrangement and it is the reason the discipline exists even inside a team that trusts itself completely, because the value of the record is realised by somebody who is not in the room. The second option overstates it, since a break narrows what can be said about the item and does not automatically exclude it, and the usual response is to corroborate the item by another route rather than to abandon it. The third confuses the two properties discussed earlier, and it is worth holding them apart: the digest chain says the content has not changed, and a custody break does not touch that at all, so the item's contents may be perfectly sound. The fourth is a proportionate-response question rather than a rule, and a great deal of useful work is routinely done alongside a break rather than instead of it.

questions.explanation: A claim about the limits of an incident is a claim about the absence of things, and absence is the hardest thing to establish from records, because the records that would show it are exactly the ones nobody thought to look at. The check is therefore to go looking, for each system the claim excludes, for a source that would have recorded activity in it, and to note when no such source is collected at all, since that converts a claim into a known unknown rather than a fact. questions.explanation: Retention has to be weighed against what each source records, and the process logs are where that comparison bites hardest, because they are the only source here that records what was running on a machine rather than what was asked of it or what data was touched. Seven days against a window of up to 45 means that for five out of every six weeks of the possible period there is no record of what was executing anywhere in the estate, and a party who entered early and left late leaves a trace only at the two ends of that period. That is the finding to raise, and the fix is a retention change on a source whose content is worth keeping rather than a rule on a source that does not exist. The second option reads coverage as a property of the longest retention in the set, and a single source cannot cover an estate no matter how long it is kept, particularly when the question is what was running. The third is a real exposure and it is the second worst on this list. The fourth is the same error as the second with a different source, and the database's audit records say nothing whatever about what was executing.
